blurb: How well do you know your dog idioms? One round per chapter of the book. Name the idiom from its picture and its meaning.

rounds.name: It Shouldn't Happen to a Dog

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dirty Dog: A cheat with charm. A dirty dog cheats.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Caught, and showing it”?
qs.x: Hangdog: Caught, and showing it. Some words need no defining.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Sick as a Dog: Wretched, and not hiding it. English rarely settles for moderate illness.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Emptied to the bone”?
qs.x: Dog-Tired: Emptied to the bone. Some kinds of tiredness deserve a gentle word.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Black Dog: Depression’s quiet companion. No dog in the language is famous in quite this way.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Something not right”?
qs.x: Sick Puppy: Something not right. The phrase sounds almost fond at first.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Tail Between the Legs: The walk of shame. A dog tells the truth with its whole body.

qs.q: Which idiom means “No chance at all”?
qs.x: Not a Dog’s Chance: No chance at all. English does not merely note poor odds.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Barking Orders: Volume mistaken for command. To bark orders is to command in short, hard bursts—no please, no preamble, no interest in whether you've been understood, only in whether you've been obeyed.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Loud, mostly harmless”?
o: Like a Dog With a Bone
qs.x: Bark Worse Than Bite: Loud, mostly harmless. Some creatures specialize in theatrical menace.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Like a Dog With a Bone
qs.x: All Bark and No Bite: Threat you can take off. This expression cuts no slack.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Certain, and certainly wrong”?
qs.x: Barking Up the Wrong Tree: Certain, and certainly wrong. The phrase comes from hunting dogs making fools of themselves in the dark.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: The Dog Who Didn’t Bark: The telling silence. Most idioms describe something happening.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Unable to let go”?
o: Like a Dog With a Bone
qs.x: Like a Dog With a Bone: Unable to let go. Some pursuits stop being reasonable long before they stop being energetic.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Barking Mad: Cheerfully unhinged. English owns a great many words for madness.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Moves On”?
qs.x: The Dogs Bark, the Caravan: Moves On. Noise the powerful ignore Object as loudly as you like.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Puppy Love: Youthful or innocent infatuation. Adults smile at it.

qs.q: Which idiom means “A pleadingly persuasive expression”?
qs.x: Puppydog Eyes: A pleadingly persuasive expression. Dogs worked out manipulation long before humans admitted it had a name.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Lapdog: A weak, dependent, submissive person. Few insults sound this soft while landing this hard.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Associate with bad company and suffer”?
qs.x: Lie Down With Dogs: Associate with bad company and suffer. The warning is old because the mistake is old.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: In the Doghouse: In disgrace or emotional exile. Few places in the language are colder.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Under close control or limited freedom”?
qs.x: On a Short Leash: Under close control or limited freedom. Trust gives free rein.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Howling at the Moon: Longing and loneliness. Not every howl is anger.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The loyalty between humans and dogs”?
qs.x: Man’s Best Friend: The loyalty between humans and dogs. This one is less idiom than verdict.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dog Days of Summer: The hottest, slowest stretch of summer. Some heat destroys ambition.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Raining extremely heavily”?
qs.x: Raining Cats and Dogs: Raining extremely heavily. English could have settled for heavy rain.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Three-Dog Night: Cold measured in dogs. Some idioms remember survival more vividly than comfort.

qs.q: Which idiom means “To labor extremely hard”?
qs.x: Work Like a Dog: To labor extremely hard. Not all exhaustion earns admiration.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dog It: To avoid effort; to loaf. Every workplace has one virtuoso of strategic underperformance.

qs.q: Which idiom means “To swim clumsily but persistently”?
qs.x: Dog Paddle: To swim clumsily but persistently. The dog paddle is not elegant.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Snapping at Heels: Pursuing closely and aggressively. Some pursuit runs on irritation, not ambition.

qs.q: Which idiom means “To compete at the highest level”?
qs.x: Run With the Big Dogs: To compete at the highest level. The phrase flatters ambition while quietly threatening humiliation.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dog-Eat-Dog: Ruthlessly competitive. Some environments strip civilization down to appetite.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The strongest eats first”?
qs.x: Let the Big Dog Eat: The strongest eats first. Hierarchy stops pretending eventually.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Hot Dog: All swagger, all performance. Some people crave applause almost as intensely as survival.

qs.q: Which idiom means “A scrap offered as mercy”?
qs.x: Throw a Bone: A scrap offered as mercy. Sometimes power offers mercy in pieces.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Eat Your Own Dogfood: Taste what you sell. Modern business culture produced many ugly expressions.

qs.q: Which idiom means “A drink taken to cure a hangover”?
qs.x: Hair of the Dog: A drink taken to cure a hangover. Some bad decisions disguise themselves as solutions.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dog’s Breakfast: A complete mess. Some failures scatter themselves across a room immediately.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Overdressed to the point of farce”?
qs.x: Dog’s Dinner: Overdressed to the point of farce. Unlike a dog’s breakfast, a dog’s dinner tries too hard.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: Dog Whistle: A message only some can hear. The whistle was once literal.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Pursuit that never rests”?
o: The Dogs Are at the Door
qs.x: Hound Someone: Pursuit that never rests. Hounds were bred to pursue tirelessly, across impossible distances.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: The Dogs Are at the Door
A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: Dogged Pursuit: Persistence as a weapon. Not brilliance.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Violence, outsourced”?
o: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: Set the Dogs on Someone: Violence, outsourced. Once the dogs were real.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: The Dogs Are at the Door
A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: The Dogs Are at the Door: Trouble, still outside. Pressure announces itself before it enters.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Decline, romanticized”?
o: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: Gone to the Dogs: Decline, romanticized. The phrase once meant visible decline—rack and ruin: property collapsing, families weakening, institutions rotting.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit: We repeat what shames us. The phrase appears in Proverbs.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Ending the chase”?
o: A Dog Returns to Its Vomit
qs.x: Call Off the Dogs: Ending the chase. Every pursuit reaches a point where continuing becomes excessive.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dogfight: Close, no room for speeches. Originally literal, dogfight meant dogs fighting for blood, money, and spectacle.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Conflict as weather”?
qs.x: Fighting Like Cats and Dogs: Conflict as weather. Some relationships survive entirely through friction.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Top Dog: Eats first, sleeps lightly. Hierarchy dislikes ambiguity.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Weakness with teeth”?
qs.x: Underdog: Weakness with teeth. People claim to admire winners.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: No Dog in This Fight: No stake, no reason to bleed. Neutrality becomes difficult once fighting starts.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The crowd, all at once”?
qs.x: Dogpile: The crowd, all at once. A dogpile begins with one body underneath.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Thrown to the Dogs: Sacrificed to save the rest. Civilization protects people conditionally.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Violence, once unleashed”?
qs.x: Dogs of War: Violence, once unleashed. Shakespeare gave the phrase its teeth: “Cry ‘Havoc!’”, and let slip the dogs of war.” The line survived because war behaves exactly like released animals.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Dog’s Age: Longer than it should be. Some stretches of time feel biological.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Tired, and barely paid”?
qs.x: A Dog’s Life: Tired, and barely paid. Not every hard life looks tragic from the outside.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Old Dog, New Tricks: Habit hardens with age. People enjoy quoting this phrase at others.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Pride mistaken for toughness”?
qs.x: Mad Dogs and Englishmen: Pride mistaken for toughness. No empire ever considered itself irrational.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Let Sleeping Dogs Lie: Leave old trouble alone. Some problems improve through neglect.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Forced back into obedience”?
qs.x: Bring to Heel: Forced back into obedience. The phrase comes straight from dog training.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Living Dog Is Better Than a Dead Lion
qs.x: A Living Dog Is Better Than a Dead Lion: Survival beats glory. The proverb comes from Ecclesiastes: “A living dog is better than a dead lion.” Ancient cultures admired lions and despised dogs.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Die wretchedly, in shame, alone”?
qs.x: Die Like a Dog: Die wretchedly, in shame, alone. The phrase is turned for contempt.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Put On the Dog: To dress or behave extravagantly. Some displays of wealth are less about pleasure than announcement.

qs.q: Which idiom means “A flashy but shallow presentation”?
qs.x: Dog and Pony Show: A flashy but shallow presentation. A dog and pony show promises amazement loudly.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: See a Man About a Dog
qs.x: Tail Wagging the Dog: The lesser controlling the greater. Hierarchy occasionally reverses itself.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The journey is the joke”?
o: See a Man About a Dog
qs.x: Shaggy Dog Story: The journey is the joke. Some stories survive precisely because they waste time magnificently.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: See a Man About a Dog
qs.x: See a Man About a Dog: An exit that explains nothing. Some departures improve through vagueness.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Something exceptionally good”?
qs.x: Dog’s Bollocks: Something exceptionally good. British English occasionally produces phrases impossible to defend logically.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Lucky Dog: A fortunate person. Luck embarrasses ambitious people.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Everyone gets the moment he deserves”?
o: See a Man About a Dog
qs.x: Every Dog Has His Day: Everyone gets the moment he deserves. The phrase comes from antiquity and passed through Shakespeare before settling into common speech.
